summary: Describes using elliptic curve algorithms, ECDH with EnvelopedData and ECDSA with SignedData, to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type in CMS. It extends RFC 5959 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Says how to use compact math locks and signatures when sending a package holding a private key.

subtitle: Adds elliptic curve ECDH and ECDSA as options for protecting asymmetric key packages in CMS.

tldr.problem: RFC 5959 lists algorithms for protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with CMS, but it did not include Elliptic Curve algorithms for SignedData and EnvelopedData.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6162 says implementations MAY support ECDSA with SignedData and standard ECDH with EnvelopedData, and MUST support keys on the P-256 curve if they support either.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new algorithms and extends RFC 5959. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6162 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5959. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5959 describes how Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) can protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type from RFC 5958. It covers SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData.

RFC 6162 amends RFC 5959 by extending the algorithms used with SignedData and EnvelopedData to include ECDSA and ECDH. It defines no new algorithms; it refers to previously defined ones.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a list of ways to protect a box of keys. This note adds two more ways to the list.

sections.title: SignedData and EnvelopedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports SignedData, then it MAY support the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), as defined in RFC 6090 and RFC 5753.

For EnvelopedData, when key agreement is used, standard (as opposed to cofactor) Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) MAY be supported. Both are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing the box proves who sent it, and the ECDH lock lets two people agree on a secret. Both are allowed, but you do not have to use them.

sections.title: Public Key Sizes
sections.content:
The easiest way to implement SignedData and EnvelopedData is with public key certificates, as profiled in RFC 5280 and RFC 5480.

If an implementation supports ECDSA or ECDH, then it MUST support keys on the P-256 curve.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who uses these tools must at least understand one standard key size, so they can talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no security text of its own. It says the security considerations from RFC 5280, RFC 5480, RFC 5652, RFC 5753, RFC 5959 and RFC 6090 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules are in the older documents, and they still count.
